note: Hand-written worked examples. They show a way to approach a problem; they are not facts about the user's data.

examples.problem: Monthly revenue fell 18% and the owner wants to know why.
steps: Confirm the drop is real: same date range, same definition of revenue, no missing days or a late data load.
Split by segment (product, customer, channel, region) and compare each to the prior period.
Separate volume from price: orders x average order value.
Check the biggest segment moves for one-offs (a lost large customer, a refund batch).
State the finding with numbers, and what you could not check.
examples.check: Segment changes should add up to the total change; if they don't, a segment is missing.

examples.problem: A total is higher than the source system after joining two tables.
steps: Count rows before and after the join.
Check the join key is unique on the side you expected to be one row per key.
Aggregate the many-side first, then join.
Re-check the total against the source.
examples.check: Row count after the join should equal the left table's count when the right side is one row per key.

examples.problem: An A/B test shows 5.2% vs 4.8% conversion and someone wants to ship the winner.
steps: Check sample size per arm and that the split was random.
Run a two-proportion test and report the confidence interval of the difference, not only the p-value.
Compare the interval to the smallest lift that matters to the business.
Do not stop early on a good-looking day; use the sample size you planned.
Report as: lift, interval, decision, caveats.
examples.check: If the interval includes zero, say the test is inconclusive rather than calling a winner.

examples.problem: Two columns look strongly correlated and someone claims one causes the other.
steps: Plot it first and look for outliers or clusters.
Check the correlation with and without outliers, and use a rank correlation if the data is skewed.
List other variables that could drive both (season, size, time).
Say it is an association unless there was an experiment.
examples.check: A correlation that vanishes after removing one or two points is not a reliable finding.

examples.problem: Training accuracy is 99% but accuracy on new data is 70%.
steps: Check for leakage: a feature derived from the target, or rows of the same entity in both train and test.
Split by time or by entity when the real use is on new ones.
Compare with a simple baseline (majority class, linear model).
Reduce complexity or add regularisation and watch the validation score, not the training score.
Report the metric that matches the cost of mistakes (recall, precision, error in dollars).
examples.check: Fit any scaling or encoding on the training split only, then apply it to the test split.

examples.problem: Only 2% of rows are positive and the model predicts 'no' for everything with 98% accuracy.
steps: Drop accuracy as the headline metric.
Look at precision, recall and the precision-recall curve.
Choose the threshold from the cost of a miss versus a false alarm.
Try class weights before resampling, and resample only the training split.
examples.check: Compare against the baseline of always predicting the majority class.

examples.problem: A calculation gives a result that looks off by a factor of 10 or 1000.
steps: Write every input with its unit.
Convert all inputs to one consistent system before calculating.
Do a rough estimate by hand to see the right order of magnitude.
Carry units through the formula and check the result's unit is the one you expect.
State the assumptions and that a qualified engineer must verify safety-critical numbers.
examples.check: The answer's units must match the quantity asked for; if not, the formula or a conversion is wrong.

examples.problem: Choosing a part size and wanting to know how much margin is enough.
steps: List the loads and the worst case they could reach.
Find the part's rated capacity from the datasheet.
Divide capacity by worst-case load to get the margin.
Compare with the margin the standard or customer requires.
examples.check: Use the datasheet rating at the real operating conditions, not the headline number.

examples.problem: An AI feature gives confident wrong answers.
steps: Collect 10 to 20 real failing questions with the right answers.
Check whether the needed information was even given to the model.
Fix retrieval or the prompt first: give sources, ask it to say when it does not know.
Re-run the same questions and compare before and after.
Keep the question set as a regression test.
examples.check: A change counts as better only if the fixed set improves without breaking questions that already passed.

examples.problem: AI calls are too slow or too expensive.
steps: Measure tokens in and out per call and the call count.
Trim the prompt and cache what repeats.
Use a smaller model for simple steps and a larger one for hard steps.
Check quality on a test set after each change.
examples.check: Never judge a cheaper model by a few examples; use the same test set.

examples.problem: A project is slipping and the client keeps adding requests.
steps: List what was agreed in writing.
List each new request with its effort estimate.
Show the effect on the date, and offer the choices: add time, add cost, or swap something out.
Get the decision in writing before continuing.
examples.check: Every change should have an owner, a date impact and a yes or no.

examples.problem: Writing a weekly status for a non-technical client.
steps: Start with overall status in one line (on track, at risk, late) and why.
Done this week, next week, blockers and what you need from them.
Keep dates and numbers specific.
Name the top risk with the plan for it.
examples.check: A reader should be able to act after the first three lines.

examples.problem: A request says 'make the report better'.
steps: Ask who uses it and what decision it supports.
Turn each wish into a testable statement: given, when, then.
List what is out of scope.
Confirm the list with the requester.
examples.check: Each requirement must be something a person could check as done or not done.

examples.problem: Mapping a manual process that is slow and error-prone.
steps: Write the steps as they happen today, including workarounds.
Mark each handoff and where data is retyped.
Time the waiting steps.
Pick the one change that removes the most waiting or retyping.
examples.check: Walk the map with someone who does the work; they will find steps you missed.

examples.problem: A user clicked a link in a suspicious email and entered their password.
steps: Change the password now from a clean device and sign out all sessions.
Turn on multi-factor authentication.
Check the account's mail rules, forwarding and recent sign-ins.
Check where else that password was used and change those.
Report it to whoever owns the account and note what happened.
examples.check: Look for forwarding rules and added recovery details; attackers use them to stay in.

examples.problem: A computer shows signs of ransomware.
steps: Disconnect it from the network but leave it powered on.
Do not pay or delete anything yet; photograph the message.
Identify what was reachable from it (shares, backups).
Restore from a backup you have verified is clean and offline.
Find how it got in before reconnecting.
examples.check: Treat other machines on the same network as suspect until checked.

examples.problem: Internet is slow for everyone on the network.
steps: Test a wired connection to see if it is Wi-Fi or the line.
Ping the router, then an outside address, and note loss and time.
Test a lookup by IP and by name to separate DNS from the connection.
Restart the modem and router, then check channel crowding on Wi-Fi.
If the wired speed is below the plan, call the provider with the test times.
examples.check: Change one thing at a time and re-test, or you won't know what fixed it.

examples.problem: Two devices have the same IP address.
steps: Find the conflicting address and both devices' MAC addresses.
Check whether one device is set to a static address inside the DHCP range.
Move static devices outside the DHCP range or reserve them in the router.
Renew the lease on the other device.
examples.check: Document the final address plan so the conflict doesn't return.

examples.problem: A laptop is very slow after startup.
steps: Check free disk space and memory use in Task Manager.
Check startup programs and disable the unneeded.
Check disk health and run updates and a malware scan.
If it still crawls, consider an SSD or more memory.
Back up the data before any bigger change.
examples.check: Record what you changed in the fix log so the next case starts from it.

examples.problem: A printer shows offline and nothing prints.
steps: Check power, paper and the cable or network link.
Clear the print queue and restart the print spooler.
Reinstall or update the driver.
Make sure the printer has a fixed address and the computer points to it.
examples.check: Print a test page from the printer itself to separate printer from computer.

examples.problem: A digital design works in simulation but fails on hardware.
steps: Check the clock and reset reach every part and are not gated oddly.
Look for signals crossing clock domains without synchronisers.
Compare simulation timing assumptions with the real timing report.
Add a probe or counter at the failing point and compare.
examples.check: Simulation does not show metastability or timing violations unless you test them.

examples.problem: A sensor reading is noisy on a microcontroller.
steps: Check power supply noise and the ground connection.
Add a small capacitor close to the sensor and average several samples.
Make sure the source impedance suits the ADC input.
Calibrate against a known reference.
examples.check: Compare readings with a meter before blaming the code.

examples.problem: The frontend calls the API and gets an error.
steps: Open the browser network tab and read the status and response.
Reproduce the same request with curl or a test.
Read the backend log for the matching error.
Check CORS, the URL and the data shape.
Fix it and add a test that fails without the fix.
examples.check: A 4xx points at the request, a 5xx at the server; start on the right side.

examples.problem: Reviewing a form handler that builds a SQL string from user input.
steps: Find where user text enters a query.
Replace string building with parameterised queries.
Validate type and length on the server, not only in the browser.
Add a test with a quote character in the input.
examples.check: Never trust client-side checks; the server must enforce them.
